topIssues.title: op-node/op-geth: post-exec (0x7D) tx payload not validated on decode (latent Go↔Rust divergence)
topIssues.author: sebastianst
topIssues.body:
Found during independent review of #21907. Inherited op-geth design, not introduced there — another instance of the known Go-lenient/Rust-strict wire-divergence class (cf. brotli strictness), reachable only via a misbehaving sequencer/batcher.

## Divergence

The post-exec (`0x7D`, `PostExecTx`) transaction's `Data` payload is treated as **opaque bytes on the Go side** and **parsed + validated on the Rust side**:

- **Go** — op-geth `core/types/post_exec_tx.go` `decode()` is `CopyBytes` (no parse); `op-core/types.PostExecTx` validates only the type byte + non-empty payload; op-node derivation frames it opaquely (singular batch: type byte + SDM gate only; span batch: `rlp.Stream.Raw()`). Nothing in the Go consensus path reads the payload's contents.
- **Rust** — op-alloy `TxPostExec` / `PostExecPayload::from_rlp_bytes` requires `version == POST_EXEC_PAYLOAD_VERSION`, canonical RLP, and no trailing bytes; a malformed payload is rejected at decode.

So a block / span-batch carrying a post-exec tx with a malformed payload (wrong version / non-canonical inner RLP / trailing bytes) is accepted by the Go stack but rejected by op-alloy/kona at decode — a potential op-node↔kona derivation divergence.

## Confirmed Go-side impact

Investigated whether a malformed payload later triggers a Go-side execution error (which would close the gap). Findings against the current op-geth pin (`v1.101702.3-rc.5`):

1. **The Go consensus/derivation path never validates payload content — anywhere.** This is the durable finding: `PostExecTxType` appears only in op-geth `core/types/*`, and nothing between op-node derivation and the engine reads the payload bytes.
2. **The "Go accepts a block kona rejects" divergence is NOT reachable _today_ — but only accidentally.** In op-geth rc.5, post-exec execution is not wired: a `0x7D` tx becomes a message with `to=nil`, `gasFeeCap=0`, `gasLimit=0` and fails EL `preCheck` (`ErrFeeCapTooLow`; `ErrIntrinsicGas` on a zero-basefee chain) **independent of payload content** (`core/state_transition.go:410-413,539-545`; signer returns the zero address for `0x7D`, `core/types/transaction_signing.go:274-276`). Every block containing a post-exec tx is therefore rejected by the Go EL, valid or malformed. Go rejects at the _execution_ stage for an unrelated reason, not because it validates the payload.
3. **The divergence becomes real the moment Go EL SDM execution is wired**, unless payload validation is added on the Go side. It is a latent, pre-SDM-execution issue, not exploitable against the current stack.

Per-category detail (relevant once Go execution accepts these blocks):

| Malformation | Go derivation | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Wrong version byte | accepted | never checked |
| Non-canonical inner RLP | accepted | the outer list header _is_ caught on the span-batch path by geth's `rlp.Stream` (`ErrCanonSize` + list-kind requirement); inner-item non-minimality is not; the singular-batch path is fully opaque |
| Trailing bytes | accepted (singular batch) | not representable in a span batch — the payload's outer RLP header self-frames the tx, so appended bytes are consumed as the next tx |

## Related open question

op-revm's `catch_error` currently lumps `PostExec` into the collapsed non-deposit "discard-and-continue" arm (raised by @geoknee in review of #21723). Whether a tx-validity error is even legitimately reachable for a `0x7D` tx is a separate open decision that interacts with this one: if these txs are producer-generated and a validity error implies a consensus bug, both stacks should agree on halting vs. continuing.

## Possible resolutions

- Align op-geth / op-core to validate the payload on decode (strict), matching op-alloy — preferred if the payload format is fixed; or
- Explicitly spec the opaque treatment and relax the Rust side.

The op-core golden vectors in #21931 pin only the hash/encoding of _valid_ payloads, not the acceptance boundary — whichever way this is resolved should add acceptance-boundary vectors shared across the Go and Rust suites.

🤖 *Co-created with Claude Fable 5*

topIssues.title: op-node: block building delayed up to 2 seconds during L1 batch derivation
topIssues.author: akundaz
topIssues.body:
**Bug Description**
When L1 batches arrive for derivation, the sequencer's FCU w/attr call can be delayed by nearly 2 seconds, causing blocks to be produced late.

This can delay the subsequent block too and this makes producing the expected number of flashblocks unfeasible. 

**Steps to Reproduce**
1. Clone the [builder-playground repo](https://github.com/flashbots/builder-playground)
    ```
    git clone git@github.com:flashbots/builder-playground.git
    ```
2. Start the opstack recipe in builder-playground with the 
    ```
    go run . cook opstack \
        --flashblocks \
        --external-builder http://host.docker.internal:4444 \
        --block-time 1 \
        --batcher-max-channel-duration 50
    ```
   This will run the default op-node version in builder-playground, which is `v1.16.3`. 
3. Wait 10 minutes (50 L1 blocks) for the derivation pipeline to run
4. Filter rollup-boost logs for lines that contain "Sending fork_choice_updated_v3 to builder" and "timestamp=Some(1771637243)". Note how the timestamp (of when the log is printed) is very close to the second boundary nearly all the time, but when the L1 batch derivation pipeline runs, the timestamp is delayed, usually in the hundreds of milliseconds.

Optional: I also tested this out against HEAD. To do this compile op-node locally, then point builder-playground to the new binary
```
# In optimism repo
cd op-node
just op-node

# In builder-playground repo
go run . cook opstack \
    .... same flags as before \
    --override op-node=/path/to/op-node/binary/like/optimism/op-node/bin/op-node
```
This has the advantage of being able to test potential op-node fixes easily or add new debug logs. For example, I modified `onBuildStart` in `op-node/rollup/engine/build_start.go` to print the delays in op-node to easier inspect delays:
```
func (e *EngineController) onBuildStart(ctx context.Context, ev BuildStartEvent) {
	eventReceivedTime := time.Now()
	rpcCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(e.ctx, buildStartTimeout)
	defer cancel()

	// Calculate slot delay: how late are we compared to when we should start building?
	// We should start building at (block_timestamp - block_time)
	// slot_delay_ms = actual_start - expected_start
	// Positive = late, Negative = early, ~0 = on time
	blockTimestamp := time.Unix(int64(ev.Attributes.Attributes.Timestamp), 0)
	expectedStart := blockTimestamp.Add(-time.Duration(e.rollupCfg.BlockTime) * time.Second)
	slotDelayMs := eventReceivedTime.Sub(expectedStart).Milliseconds()

	e.log.Info("BuildStartEvent received",
		"block_number", ev.Attributes.Parent.Number+1,
		"slot_delay_ms", slotDelayMs)

    ...rest of function unchanged
```

**Expected behavior**
Desired behavior is for FCU w/attr to come reliably at the same time each second.

**Environment Information:**
Local testing on mac. We see this in all our environments running linux.
Tested op-node versions `v1.16.3` and `a439b465` (my current head commit).

**Configurations:**
`--batcher-max-channel-duration 50`. This doesn't show up reliably if I set this value low, which makes sense because derivation is much quicker then.

**Logs:**
<!--
Logs and/or error messages that help illustrate the issue.
-->
Log sample from running op-node with the additional print statement from above (filtered and truncated):
```
t=2026-02-20T21:17:41-0500 lvl=info msg="BuildStartEvent received" block_number=612 slot_delay_ms=11
..
t=2026-02-20T21:17:42-0500 lvl=info msg="BuildStartEvent received" block_number=613 slot_delay_ms=5
..
repeated 600 times:
lvl=info msg="decoded singular batch from channel"
lvl=info msg="generated attributes in payload queue"
..
t=2026-02-20T21:17:43-0500 lvl=info msg="BuildStartEvent received" block_number=614 slot_delay_ms=217
..
t=2026-02-20T21:17:44-0500 lvl=info msg="BuildStartEvent received" block_number=615 slot_delay_ms=4

```

**Additional context**
I initially thought https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/issues/15393 would be a contributing factor, but adding debouncing (via https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/pull/18385) did not get rid of the delay. 

I suspect the root cause is that the `EngineController` holds a lock while making blocking RPC calls:
```
func (e *EngineController) OnEvent(ctx context.Context, ev event.Event) bool {
	e.mu.Lock()
	defer e.mu.Unlock()
	// ... blocking RPC calls while holding lock
}
```
During batch derivation hundreds of events are emitted and the FCU w/attr call would need to wait for all of them, which could cause such a delay.

topIssues.title: [PCD Milestone 3] op-deployer & Tooling Runbook
topIssues.author: 0xiamflux
topIssues.body:
## Context
The PCD introduces changes to `op-deployer`, including a new pipeline and additional requirements for `intent.json`. As a result, consumers of the pipeline need to understand the step-by-step process and the actionable items needed to recover from the different input validation failures.

## Definition of Done

The deliverable for this issue is a document that can be used as a runbook to take a permissionless deployment live on-chain, either using `op-deployer` directly for simpler setups or the companion tooling to coordinate multi-chain setups.

topIssues.title: op-acceptance-tests: TestProposerDefendsMultipleChallengedGamesConcurrently flakes on kona-sp1-proposer metrics port collision
topIssues.author: maurelian
topIssues.body:
`TestProposerDefendsMultipleChallengedGamesConcurrently` flakes with the proposer dying on boot:

```
kona-sp1-proposer | Error: failed to start metrics server:
  failed to create HTTP listener: Address already in use (os error 98)

Error Trace:  op-devstack/sysgo/zk_proposer.go:249
              op-devstack/sysgo/multichain_proofs.go:115
              op-acceptance-tests/tests/proofs/zk/zk_dispute_game_test.go:218
Error:        kona-sp1-proposer exited before its startup line was emitted
Test:         TestProposerDefendsMultipleChallengedGamesConcurrently
```

Seen in `memory-all-opn-op-reth-prague` ([build 5436840](https://app.circleci.com/pipelines/github/ethereum-optimism/optimism/jobs/5436840)). It took down `ci-gate`, which lists that job as `terminal`, so it blocks merge on an unrelated PR (#22290).

## Cause

`op-acceptance-tests/tests/proofs/zk/zk_dispute_game_test.go:252` is the F15 anti-pattern from [docs/ai/flake-prevention.md](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/develop/docs/ai/flake-prevention.md#f15--selecting-a-free-port-before-starting-the-service):

```go
func freeTCPPort(t devtest.T) uint16 {
	listener, err := net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0")
	t.Require().NoError(err, "reserve an ephemeral port")
	defer listener.Close()   // port released here
	return uint16(listener.Addr().(*net.TCPAddr).Port)
}
```

The port is released as soon as it's read, then passed to `kona-sp1-proposer` via `METRICS_PORT`. The proposer doesn't bind it until after `NewSimpleInterop` has stood up L1, the supernode, batchers, proposers and challengers — a multi-second window in which the kernel can hand that same number to any other socket. The number is drawn from the ephemeral range that every other socket in the process also draws from, and `#22208` (`op-acceptance-tests: run ZK dispute game tests in parallel`) put many more sockets in flight concurrently, which is what turned a latent race into an observed flake.

## Fixing it

Per F15, the owner of the socket should bind port 0 and report its address, rather than having the test preselect one. Two constraints make this more than a one-liner:

- `METRICS_PORT=0` currently means *metrics disabled*, and `zk_proposer.go:205-212` deliberately pins it so an inherited `METRICS_PORT` (op-succinct deployments export that exact name) can't leak into devstack proposers. So "0 = ephemeral" isn't available; the mode needs a distinct signal, e.g. `MetricsListen { Disabled, Ephemeral, Fixed(u16) }`.
- `metrics_exporter_prometheus` 0.18 binds inside `new_http_listener` and never surfaces the bound `SocketAddr`, and `with_http_listener` takes a `SocketAddr` rather than a listener — so the exporter can't report an ephemeral port, and can't adopt a listener we opened. Resolving the port inside the proposer therefore still needs a probe-then-bind, but the window collapses from seconds across processes to microseconds within one, and can be wrapped in a retry loop.

Sketch:

- `rust/kona/sp1/crates/proposer/src/config.rs` — parse `METRICS_PORT` into a three-state mode.
- `rust/kona/sp1/crates/host/src/metrics.rs` — `init_metrics` returns the resolved `SocketAddr`, retrying on `AddrInUse` in ephemeral mode.
- `rust/kona/sp1/crates/proposer/src/bin/kona-sp1-proposer.rs` — log the resolved address in the existing `metrics_addr` field of the `kona-sp1-proposer started` line.
- `op-devstack/sysgo/zk_proposer.go` — the startup-line callback already parses that log entry; capture `metrics_addr` and expose it.
- `op-acceptance-tests/tests/proofs/zk/zk_dispute_game_test.go` — drop `freeTCPPort`, scrape the reported address.

A cheaper interim mitigation, if the cross-language change isn't wanted yet: keep the preselection but make it recoverable — on `Address already in use`, pick a fresh port and restart the proposer. That leaves the race in place but makes residual failure negligible.

`freeTCPPort` has one caller today, so the blast radius either way is small.

topPRs.title: op-node: run sequencer on its own goroutine
topPRs.author: sebastianst
topPRs.body:
Eliminates sequencer starvation by the shared event loop: block production no longer competes with derivation for the driver thread. Stacked on #22238.

The sequencer emits no events on the block-production path. It calls the engine controller directly (`StartBuild`/`SealBuild`/`ProcessPayload` from #22238) and paces itself with its own timer in `RunLoop`, on a dedicated goroutine started by the driver. Sequencer latency under derivation load drops from "full event-queue drain" (seconds during span-batch consolidation, #19263) to at most one in-flight `e.mu` critical section.

**Ingestion — ordered mailbox.** External signals (forkchoice updates, resets, temp errors, derivation build activity, derivation-processed payloads) arrive via the retained ingest-only Deriver registration: `OnEvent` appends to an ordered log under a micro-mutex and fires a cap-1 wake channel — it never blocks the event loop and never mutates sequencer state. The goroutine replays entries in arrival order through the existing handlers; adjacent non-rewinding forkchoice updates coalesce to the latest. Replay-then-decide: an action fire first drains the inbox and honors a schedule parked by the replay.

**Error discipline — park-and-echo.** Every error path that defers recovery to an event echoing back through the mailbox parks the schedule first (`nextActionOK=false`); paths with no echo (`ErrBuildInvalid`, seal errors, undecodable gossip payload) back off locally. `RunLoop` never re-arms an already-fired deadline, so no-op actions cannot spin.

**Driver.** `planSequencerAction`, `sequencerTimer`, `sequencerCh`, `SequencerActionEvent`, and `SequencerIface.NextAction` are deleted; `Driver.Start` launches `RunLoop`. Lock order is strictly `d.l → e.mu`; the event thread holds neither when calling the other side. Also deletes the `attributes.go` sequencer-origin gates on seal errors, which are now only emitted for derived builds.

**Fan-out unchanged**: error events (reset/temporary/critical) are still emitted (enqueue is thread-safe); the derivation-origin build event chain, conductor, and async gossip are untouched.

Tests: unit + chaos rework to direct calls; new inbox tests (arrival-order replay, rewind-safe coalescing, wake coalescing, RunLoop liveness incl. the start/stop wake contracts of #22145, which this supersedes); action-test helpers call `RunAction` synchronously. Design reviewed adversarially by two independent passes; every finding is fixed with a pinning regression test.

Supersedes #22145. Closes #19263, #22232

🤖 *Co-created with Claude (Fable 5)*

topPRs.title: Lagoon hardfork rename (cherry-pick of #21105)
topPRs.author: maurelian
topPRs.body:
Cherry-picks #21105 (`b5c39b2`) onto `proposal/op-contracts/v7.0.0`.

The branch diverged from `develop` around 2026-05-01, so 36 of the 101 files
conflicted. Resolution rule throughout: keep the v7.0.0 side of each conflict,
then re-apply the rename to whatever v7.0.0 actually has. Nine files in the
upstream diff were added to `develop` after the divergence and don't exist here
(`op-node/rollup/derive/interop_activation_transactions.go`, the `sdm` acceptance
tests, `rust/op-rbuilder/*`, …); those were dropped rather than reintroduced.

The Rust conflicts were redone from the v7.0.0 files rather than merged, because
the keep-ours pass left `pub struct Lagoon` next to `impl Interop`. The
consensus-critical `UpgradeDepositSource` intent strings (`"Interop: …"`) are
deliberately untouched — only type paths were renamed.

The second commit fixes call sites that only exist on v7.0.0, so the upstream PR
had no equivalent of them to rename. Note `IsInterop`/`IsInteropActivationBlock`
on the op-supervisor depset config types keep their names: those are the
concept-level interop interface, not the fork.

Verified: `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, gofmt clean; `cargo check --workspace
--all-targets` and `cargo +nightly fmt --check` clean; kona crates touched by the
rename pass with `--all-features`. Go test failures under `op-deployer`/`op-node/p2p`
are identical to those on the unmodified base branch (they need built contract
artifacts).

topPRs.title: contracts-bedrock: Super ZK Dispute Game Internal Review Remediations
topPRs.author: 0xarktos
topPRs.body:
## Summary

Remediates internal review findings on the Super ZK dispute game. Adds a solvency invariant and a migration boundary test for `ZKDisputeGame`, and bounds the ZK durations in `OPContractsManagerStandardValidator` and `op-deployer`. No core contract changes are introduced.

## Review Issues Remediated

| Issue | Description | Remediation |
|---|---|---|
| `M-03` | `ZKDisputeGame` had no fuzz or invariant coverage. Bond conservation across `resolve()` was checked only by hand written examples. | Added `ZKDisputeGame_Solvency_Invariant` with a `RandomZKActor` harness. |
| `M-04` | The SFDG to ZKDG migration was only tested against a clean pre state. No game, anchor or blacklist entry ever crossed the flip. | Added `test_flip_inFlightStateCrossesBoundary_succeeds`. |
| `F-05` | ZK durations had no upper bound. A value near `uint64` max truncates the deadline cast, so the game is over the instant it is created and resolves `DEFENDER_WINS` unproven. | Bounded both durations at `type(uint32).max` in `_assertValidZKGameArgs` and both `op-deployer` encoders. |

## Detailed Changes

### `[M-03]` No fuzz or invariant coverage

Added `test/invariants/ZKDisputeGame.t.sol`, modelled on the `SuperFaultDisputeGame` solvency invariant.

`RandomZKActor` exposes `challenge`, `prove`, `proveAsProposer` and `warpForward`, all guarded so the actor never reverts. The invariant drives the resulting state through `resolve`, the finality airgap, `closeGame` and the two phase `DelayedWETH` claim, then asserts the game holds no ETH and that the sum returned to participants equals `totalBonds`.

Conservation of the total is asserted rather than per actor balances, so the check stays branch agnostic.

The `address(0)` burn branch and REFUND mode are out of scope for this harness. Both need state the actor cannot reach.

---

### `[M-04]` Upgrade transition never exercised with in flight state

Added `test_flip_inFlightStateCrossesBoundary_succeeds` to `ZKDisputeGameSuperMigration.t.sol`.

Three pieces of pre boundary state cross the real `OPCMv2.upgrade()` flip. A game that already advanced the anchor, a blacklisted game, and a game left `IN_PROGRESS`.

The test pins the value level result of the in place ASR re initialization. `anchorGame` is cleared, `retirementTimestamp` and the blacklist survive, and the unresolved game still resolves, closes in NORMAL mode and re advances the anchor. That last assertion records existing behavior, since the respected type is snapshotted at creation.

SFDG only. `SuperPermissionedDisputeGame` resolves at initialization and cannot be left in flight.

---

### `[F-05]` ZK durations have no upper bound

`_assertValidZKGameArgs` bounds both durations on the existing error codes.

```solidity
args.maxChallengeDuration > 0 && args.maxChallengeDuration <= type(uint32).max
```

`type(uint32).max` is roughly 136 years, low enough that `block.timestamp + duration` cannot approach `uint64`, so the truncation is unreachable. Validator bumped to `3.1.0` and `semver-lock.json` regenerated.

The same bound was added to `encodeZKGameArgs` and `EncodedUpgradeInputV2` in `op-deployer`, so a bad duration fails when the bundle is built. Tests pin the bound as inclusive.

`ZKDisputeGame` itself is unchanged, so a config installed outside these paths still reaches the chain.

### `[M-04]` Upgrade transition never exercised with in flight state

Added `test_flip_inFlightStateCrossesBoundary_succeeds` to `ZKDisputeGameSuperMigration.t.sol`.

Three pieces of pre boundary state cross the real `OPCMv2.upgrade()` flip. A game that already advanced the anchor, a blacklisted game, and a game left `IN_PROGRESS`.

The test pins the value level result of the in place ASR re initialization. `anchorGame` is cleared, `retirementTimestamp` and the blacklist survive, and the unresolved game still resolves, closes in NORMAL mode and re advances the anchor. That last assertion records existing behavior, since the respected type is snapshotted at creation.

SFDG only. `SuperPermissionedDisputeGame` resolves at initialization and cannot be left in flight.

---

### `[F-05]` ZK durations have no upper bound

`_assertValidZKGameArgs` bounds both durations on the existing error codes.

```solidity
args.maxChallengeDuration > 0 && args.maxChallengeDuration <= type(uint32).max
```

`type(uint32).max` is roughly 136 years, low enough that `block.timestamp + duration` cannot approach `uint64`, so the truncation is unreachable. Validator bumped to `3.1.0` and `semver-lock.json` regenerated.

The same bound was added to `encodeZKGameArgs` and `EncodedUpgradeInputV2` in `op-deployer`, so a bad duration fails when the bundle is built. Tests pin the bound as inclusive.

`ZKDisputeGame` itself is unchanged, so a config installed outside these paths still reaches the chain.

## Notes

Findings assessed and deliberately not remediated.

- **`l2SequenceNumber` has no upper bound.** A game at `uint64` max that finalized as `DEFENDER_WINS` would pin the anchor there and block all future game creation for every chain in the set. `l2SequenceNumber` is committed to the verifier through `publicValues`, so no valid proof can exist for such a game unless the timestamp being proven is exactly that value, which is not practically reachable. An unchallenged game still resolves `DEFENDER_WINS` without a proof, so this rests on a challenger acting within `maxChallengeDuration`, the same assumption every other invalid proposal relies on.
- **Game args reach the chain unvalidated on the migration paths.** `setInteropDisputeGames()` and `migrate()` never call `_assertValidFullConfig`. All parameters are validated in the `op-deployer` CLI that produces the Safe transaction calldata, and signers are expected to verify them, so tooling plus signer review is deemed sufficient.

topPRs.title: nuts: declare activation-block extra gas in the bundle schema
topPRs.author: sebastianst
topPRs.body:
Bundles now declare the gas their activation block reserves for upgrade deposits the consensus layer emits *outside* the bundle, as `metadata.extraGas`. Both readers fold it into the bundle's total gas.

For Lagoon that is the `setFeature(INTEROP)` and `ETHLiquidity` funding wrappers (150,000). Neither is expressible as a bundle transaction: the funding deposit carries a non-zero mint, and both are emitted only by a multi-chain dependency set. So the amount was hardcoded separately in op-node and kona — `UpgradeTransactions` and `UpgradeGas` return different numbers for the same fork ([footgun](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/pull/22216#discussion_r3723616297)), and the two clients can drift. #22216 fixed the drift; this removes the place it can come from.

**This PR changes no gas.** No bundle declares `extraGas` yet — see the follow-up below.

## Where the value lives

A constant beside `UPGRADE_NAME` in `GenerateNUTBundle.s.sol`, not a `just` argument. The generator already models which upgrade it builds (it branches on `"karst"` for the transaction count), and `nut-bundle-check` invokes `--sig 'run()'` and diffs the snapshot — an argument would have to be repeated in the justfile twice, reintroducing the duplication this removes. With a constant, `run()` stays zero-arg and `nut-bundle-check` and `nut-provenance-verify` work untouched, each locked commit regenerating with its own generator.

`fork_lock.toml` mirrors the value so it is visible without opening 350 KB of JSON; `check-nut-locks` enforces that mirror and bundle agree.

## Schema version

Bundles carrying the field declare `1.1.0`. All three readers (op-node, kona's build script, `NetworkUpgradeTxns.sol`) accept `{1.0.0, 1.1.0}` and reject a `1.0.0` bundle that declares `extraGas` — a reader predating the field would silently under-reserve the activation block's gas limit.

`1.0.0` stays accepted permanently: no generator can emit it any more, but every already-locked bundle uses it, and provenance verification regenerates each bundle with the generator of *its own* locked commit.

The generator's duplicate `BUNDLE_VERSION` is gone; `NetworkUpgradeTxns` owns it, since it both writes and validates the field.

## Follow-up: re-lock Lagoon

Landing `extraGas` in Lagoon's bundle **cannot** happen in this PR. `check-nut-locks` requires the lock's `commit` to be an ancestor of `develop`, and `nut-provenance-verify-changed.sh` regenerates any bundle whose hash changed, at that commit. A bundle carrying `extraGas` requires a generator that emits it, which is only on this branch — so the recorded commit would have to be both an ancestor of `develop` and contain a change that is not on `develop`.

Once this merges, a follow-up regenerates Lagoon on `develop` and drops the code-side wrapper-gas constants from both clients. That re-lock also picks up contract drift accumulated since `fa9974a2`: 10 of 28 transactions, +2,747,222 gas — almost entirely re-profiled `deployGasLimit` constants in `Predeploys.sol` rather than bytecode growth, dominated by `L1FeeVault` being corrected from a stale 260,550 to the 1,800,000 its three identical siblings use (#20982).

## Verification

`nut-bundle-check` (regeneration deterministic); `check-nut-locks`; Go `op-node/rollup/derive`, `op-core/nuts`, `ops/scripts/*`; Rust `kona-hardforks` + `op-alloy-consensus` (clippy and `fmt-check` clean); Solidity `NetworkUpgradeTxns`, `GenerateNUTBundle`, `PastNUTBundles`. `L2ForkUpgrade` / `L2GenesisForkUpgrade` are fork tests and skipped locally.

Stacked on #22216.

🤖 *Co-created with Claude Opus 5*
